opening: A ruler who keeps his promises may be destroyed by someone who does not. One who tries to be generous can end up taxing his people until they hate him. Machiavelli examines these predicaments with the attention of a man who has watched governments fall and lost his own position with one of them. His advice forces the question that respectable accounts of leadership often evade: what happens when the conduct that earns admiration is not the conduct that keeps you in power?

structure.title: Chapters 1–11 · Getting power is only the beginning
structure.text: Machiavelli distinguishes inherited states from newly acquired ones. A new ruler must contend with people who expected to benefit from his arrival, people loyal to the old order, and allies whose help comes with conditions.

structure.title: Chapters 12–14 · Whose soldiers are defending you?
structure.text: Mercenaries and borrowed armies promise strength while leaving the ruler dependent on someone else. Military organisation becomes a test of whether his power is actually his.

structure.title: Chapters 15–19 · When good conduct produces bad results
structure.text: Generosity can require taxes that make subjects hate their ruler. Mercy can permit disorder. Keeping promises can leave him exposed to people who break theirs. These chapters examine the uncomfortable distance between admirable intentions and their consequences.

structure.title: Chapters 20–23 · Governing through other people
structure.text: Fortresses, public reputation, ministers, and advisers offer different kinds of protection. The ruler needs reliable information while occupying a position that encourages everyone around him to flatter him.

structure.title: Chapters 24–26 · What can a ruler do about fortune?
structure.text: Machiavelli returns to the failures of Italian rulers and the limits of preparation. A method that once worked may become disastrous when circumstances change. The book closes by turning its analysis into an urgent appeal to act.

people.name: The new prince
people.text: He cannot rely on generations of obedience. He has displaced people, rewarded others, and created expectations he may be unable to satisfy. Much of the book asks how someone in this exposed position can make his rule last.

people.name: Cesare Borgia
people.text: Borgia appears as an example of calculated action under dangerous conditions. Follow what Machiavelli admires, what he thinks Borgia secured for himself, and what still depended on another person. An impressive operator can remain vulnerable.

people.name: The people and the nobles
people.role: Two sources of support with different demands
people.text: The nobles want to command; the people want to avoid oppression. Machiavelli argues that these ambitions give a ruler different problems. His advice often turns on which group he needs and what keeping its support will cost.

context.title: A fractured political world
context.text: The Italy of the book consists of competing states exposed to powerful neighbours and shifting alliances. A ruler can lose his position through military dependence, domestic opposition, or a change in someone else’s fortunes. This helps explain the urgency behind advice that can otherwise sound like a celebration of ruthlessness.

context.title: Virtù does not simply mean moral virtue
context.text: Machiavelli’s virtù includes the capacity to judge circumstances, act decisively, and secure results. It can require qualities that ordinary moral praise leaves out. English translations vary, so words such as ability, prowess, or virtue may carry this larger meaning.

context.title: Fortune can make yesterday’s wisdom fail
context.text: Fortuna includes changes a ruler cannot command. Machiavelli compares it to a flooding river: preparation can limit damage, even though it cannot prevent the rain. He also worries that people cling to the habits that made them successful after the circumstances favouring those habits have disappeared.

passages.quote: I compare her to one of those raging rivers

notice.text: Follow the money in the chapter on generosity.
notice.why: The prince wants to be seen giving, exhausts his resources, and then makes his subjects pay for the display. Machiavelli follows a praised quality through its costs. Keep asking who finances a ruler’s reputation.

passages.quote: will be compelled in the end

notice.why: The famous discussion does not give unlimited permission to terrorise. Machiavelli worries about conduct that turns obedience into hostility. Notice how much of his advice concerns avoiding the resentment a careless reading of his argument might encourage.

notice.text: Look for the people left outside each calculation.
notice.why: A measure may secure the ruler and injure someone else. Sometimes Machiavelli claims that harsh action prevents wider suffering. Examine both the proposed result and whose losses make that result possible.

notice.text: Watch how tightly he controls the permission to tell the truth.
notice.why: The prince should welcome frank advice, but from chosen advisers and on matters he asks about. The arrangement reveals a difficulty that remains unresolved by simply hiring honest people: how does someone who controls the questions discover what he has failed to ask?

passages.quote: only of those things of which he inquires
